# Standing mint slate — what confers standing, who says so, and why the argument never ends

*Design slate, 2026-08-29, `design/libations`. Generated by the
[aluminium-can slate](./aluminium-can-slate.md) § 7: the question "should
recycling confer standing?" turned out to be the whole platform's
question wearing a small hat.*

> **How consumer standing is minted is the ballgame.** With it you can
> affect change over every other element of gameplay — the vote, the
> market, the labour supply, who gets heard. Every other design decision
> is downstream of this one. — the founder, this session

The balance slate already supplies the vocabulary: *every global ledger
is a currency, and every parcel that writes to one is a **mint***
([balance-slate.md](./balance-slate.md) Part 1). Standing is a global
ledger. So the question is not whether standing is a currency — it is —
but **who holds the mint, on what conduct, at what weights, amendable by
whom.**

---

## Part 1 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Yes, it is a morality score. Say it.

Not a euphemism for one. A morality score is a ranking of persons by
conduct against a value system, and that is exactly what standing is.
Every hedge available ("it's just influence", "it's revealed
preference", "it's an engagement metric") is a way of not saying the
thing, and the project does not hedge.

What follows from saying it plainly is a **better** design, because the
question stops being *"is this a morality score?"* (yes) and becomes
*"what distinguishes an acceptable one from social credit?"* That
question has a structural answer, and it is not "ours measures nicer
things."

**The five tests.** A conduct score is defensible to the degree it has:

1. **Exit.** Can you leave, or fork? AGPL + self-host says yes. *A
   social credit system you can fork is not one.*
2. **Published weights.** *The first screen is the syllabus*
   ([measurement.md](../../measurement.md) Part 7). Conditioning
   requires opacity; publishing the weights is what makes it teaching.
3. **Amendability, and by whom.** Tier C (the polity) is legitimate;
   Tier B (whoever ships the code) is where we must be most
   conservative; Tier A should contain almost nothing behavioural.
4. **Plurality.** Many raters with different weights is a *reputation*;
   one rater with universal reach is a *score*.
5. **No coupling to unrelated goods.** If standing gates travel or
   housing, it is social credit. If it is what people think of you and
   whether they will deal with you — that is society.

Hold those five and the project is defensible in public without
flinching. Lose any of them — particularly 4 — and it is not.

## Part 2 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ The scalar is produced by the DECISION, not the ledger

The strongest argument in the session, and it overturned the position it
was aimed at.

Every binary choice — hire? lend? deal? admit? — collapses whatever
information exists into **one bit**. A scalar is just that collapse,
pre-computed. Therefore:

- **Refusing to aggregate does not prevent aggregation.** It relocates
  it to the moment of decision, where it happens anyway.
- Players will math it. A public deed ledger plus a spreadsheet is a
  rating agency. FICO was in nobody's constitution.
- And the relocated version is **worse on our own stated grounds**: a
  player-built score has *private* weights, which is precisely the
  property (test 2) that we said made scoring intolerable.

**The retraction, recorded.** An earlier formulation in this session was
*"the engine measures; the engine never values."* That is too clean to
survive contact. An engine that emits nothing aggregable does not
prevent valuation — it outsources it to whoever has the best scraper.
The corrected rule is Part 3.

## Part 3 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Plurality, not abstention

> **The engine measures and may publish. It must never be the only
> rater.**

The real world's answer to *"credit scores will exist"* was never "the
state issues one." It was, eventually and imperfectly, the FCRA
settlement: **you may build a score; the subject may see it and dispute
it; there are several bureaus.** Pluralism + disclosure + dispute rights
is the civilising structure. The absence of scores never was.

Which makes **rating agencies a player institution**, and that is far
better content than either extreme:

- Competing raters with **published weights** — the weights are the
  product, and disagreement between raters is a live political fight.
- **Rater capture is discoverable** through the provenance ledger. *Who
  funds the rater* is the same investigation as *who funded the Crying
  Indian* (can slate § 0).
- A polity may **regulate disclosure** — our FCRA, passed in-world.
- A bad rating from a rater nobody trusts lands nowhere, because **trust
  in the rater is itself renown.** The recursion is the point.
- **You can found one.**

## Part 4 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Where a scalar belongs, and where minting one is a lie

Scalars are not universal; they emerge under a specific condition —
**strangers transacting at volume with low per-transaction stakes.**
That is the market. It is why *consumer* standing gets scalarised
everywhere in the real world (eBay feedback, seller ratings, credit) and
*"is this person a good friend"* never does: friendship's decisions are
rich, repeated, and directly informed.

So the rule is not "scalar bad." It is:

> **Ship the scalar where the market condition holds. Do not manufacture
> one where it does not.**

And note what this does to the can: **a deposit converts a civic act
into a commercial one**, and that conversion is exactly the moment a
scalar becomes appropriate. The mechanism is self-consistent — the
polity, by pricing the externality, also decides that this conduct is
now the kind of thing that gets counted. Nobody had to rule on it from
outside.

## Part 5 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Two layers of argument, and only one of them is settleable

This session's argument had two layers that look alike and are not:

| | **mechanical** | **political** |
|---|---|---|
| asks | does the measure measure what it claims? | *whose work counts?* |
| examples | Goodhart, crowding-out, off-measurement collapse, validity | should bartending confer more than smithing |
| settled by | evidence, in-world, over time | deliberation — **never** |
| our standing to speak | high; this is engineering | **none beyond one vote** |

⚠ **And the trap:** mechanical arguments get *used as* political
weapons. "Crowding-out" will be cited, correctly and cynically, by
whoever benefits from not paying. Every argument in this slate will
become somebody's ammunition. That is what political arguments are made
of, and it is not a reason to withhold them — it is a reason to publish
them **in full, on both sides** (Part 9).

⚠⚠ **The bartender is not a villain.** A bartender arguing that
bartending should confer more standing is doing exactly what a polity is
*for*. Hospitality labour is systematically undervalued in real
economies; the bartender may simply be **right**. Special pleading is
ordinary interest-representation, not corruption. Any design that treats
"you benefit from this proposal" as disqualifying disqualifies everyone,
since everyone benefits from something — see the veto risk in Part 6.

## Part 6 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Legibility is the only lever we actually have

The simulation cannot resolve the political layer. It can do exactly one
thing: **make special interests legible.** That is the founder's claim
and it is correct, and it turns out to be buildable and rare.

**The distributional impact statement.** When a weight change is
proposed, the engine can compute *before the vote*:

- who gains and who loses, by name and by magnitude — because the engine
  already knows who holds which positions, which deeds, which scope;
- the standing distribution under current weights vs proposed;
- who proposed it, and their own exposure to it, from the chronicle;
- who funded any campaign for it, from the authorship ledger.

Real analogue: the **CBO score / fiscal note / regulatory impact
assessment** — "make the interest legible without resolving the
politics." Real legislatures mostly *cannot* do this; we can do it
exactly, automatically, for every proposal. It is plausibly the single
most valuable civic instrument the platform can ship, and the fights
over *its methodology* would be the same fights as the real ones, which
is the point.

⚠ **The veto risk.** Legibility must not become a technocratic veto. If
the tool becomes a way to delegitimise any proposal by anyone who
benefits, it has destroyed deliberation rather than served it. The
framing that survives:

> **Having an interest is not disqualifying. Concealing it is.**

## Part 7 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐ The pathologies are required reachable states, not caveats

*Make the simulation honest* is the governing rule, and taken seriously
it **generates** the objections as content rather than defeating them. A
scored world that does not reach these is flattering, not honest — the
same failure as an abstraction that costs nobody the activity
([uncertainty.md](../../uncertainty.md)):

- **Goodhart.** When the measure becomes the target it stops measuring.
  Scored recycling gets farmed — buy cans to return cans, manufacture
  deeds. Already a live mechanism in-world: the Michigan/Indiana
  cross-border deposit arb (can slate § 2).
- **Auditing**, which becomes a real vocation *only because* the score
  exists — the second vocation the can mints, after the collector.
- **Rater capture** (Part 3).
- **Crowding-out, as a ratchet.** Titmuss, *The Gift Relationship*
  (1970); Gneezy & Rustichini, *A Fine is a Price* (2000) — the daycare
  fines made lateness worse and stayed worse **after** the fine was
  withdrawn. A price can permanently destroy the cheaper mechanism it
  replaced.
- **Off-measurement collapse** (Part 8).

## Part 8 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Intrinsic vs extrinsic: same at the measured point, different everywhere else

The founder's challenge: *whether you recycle for intrinsic or extrinsic
reasons, the behaviour is the same — what's the difference?*

At the measured point, none. The difference is mechanical, not moral,
and it is entirely in the **unmeasured neighbourhood**:

1. ⭐⭐ **The unmeasured neighbours.** Paid per can, you return the can
   and leave the wrapper beside it. To the intrinsically motivated the
   can and the wrapper are one act; to the extrinsically motivated they
   are two, and one pays. **The commons is mostly made of unmeasured
   neighbours.**
2. **Unobserved behaviour.** Where measurement lapses — no scheme in
   this locality, nobody watching — extrinsic goes to zero and intrinsic
   does not. In a world with real partial observability (concealment,
   perception, belief are all shipped), that is *testable*, not
   philosophical.
3. **The ratchet.** Extrinsic can destroy the norm it replaced, and the
   norm does not come back.
4. **Adversarial gradient.** Extrinsic motivation produces *the
   appearance of the act at minimum cost*, which becomes fraud whenever
   fraud is cheaper. Intrinsic has no such gradient. That asymmetry is
   why scored systems need auditors and norms do not.

All four are simulable, and the lesson they deliver is one most adults
never learn: **incentives buy compliance at the measurement point and
nothing else.**

## Part 9 — ⭐⭐⭐⭐ The wiki carries the ARGUMENTS, not the conclusions

The founder's closing observation — *the argument the polity will have
is this argument, only political* — has a direct design consequence.

A player proposing a weight change should be able to find the
crowding-out argument. **Their opponent should be able to find the
revealed-preference rejoinder, stated just as well.** Both are real;
both have evidence; neither wins on the merits alone.

So the wiki stocks the **arsenal on both sides**, fairly stated — which
is *model the mechanism, never the verdict* applied to discourse instead
of to mechanics. This session's transcript is a worked example of the
shape: mechanical objection → political rejoinder → synthesis, with a
recorded retraction (Part 2) because retractions are what make an
argument trustworthy.

This is also the polity-decision-register's own commitment: *the
eventual polity inherits arguments, not just settings.*

## Part 10 — What ships, what defers, what is never ours

**Ships (small, now-ish):** deeds to the chronicle; per-scope derive as
it already works; the vocabulary of measurables kept **small and
physical**; nothing in this slate needs new kernel.

**Defers (real builds, in dependency order):** published weights as
readable content · the distributional impact statement · rater agencies
as a player institution · disclosure regulation as passable law · the
audit vocation.

**Never ours:** the weights. What conduct is worth what is a Tier C
question, and the register carries it as **open**, with both opening
arguments intact — see
[polity-decision-register.md](../../polity-decision-register.md) D9 and
Tier 3.

### ⭐⭐⭐ The three rules that outlive this slate

1. **Keep the measurable vocabulary small and physical.** We choose what
   is measurable *at all*; the polity only chooses weights. That is
   structural power no licence dissolves, because forking costs more
   than any player will pay.
2. **Prefer deeds over dispositions.** A deed is checkable and
   contestable; a disposition is an accusation.
3. **Treat every new measurable as a constitutional change, not a
   feature.**
